doc.title: Bobby Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: How recording deals work and sales
summary: Record companies call him; no contracts, mostly mail order, and he never learns sales figures.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: How does that work with jazz recording these days? You know downstairs they have a whole slew of CDs and many, many record labels. Do they call you? Or do you actively promote yourself to them?

No actually what they do is they call you. The record companies call you or I, as a leader, I’ve had three albums out as a leader on my own and the record companies have called me. And I’ve hired the musicians to be on the record. And that’s how it usually happens. If I’m making a record with Marty Grosz for instance, he would call me and then I would come to New York or if I was there at a certain time, and I would make the record with him. It’s not anything where you’re under contract with anybody or anything like that. It’s just making the records with somebody, and we try to sell them to whoever we can.
Do you ever hear about how many actual recordings are sold?
No I never hear of that.
You don’t get that kind of information?
We don’t get that kind of information. Most of them are mail order albums. But we do get reviews and press clippings from the different newspapers and magazines. They

always send us those things. But as far as the recordings go, in this type of jazz, they’re not exactly million sellers like that they have today. It would take a long time to ever get maybe to sell a hundred thousand records, fifty thousand records would take a long time in the kind of jazz that we’re playing today.
